examples.knowledge_point: Multiplying Two Matrices When They Are Conformable
examples.worked_solution:
Here, $C$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix and $D$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. 

There are $3$ columns in $C$ and $3$ rows in $D,$ so $C$ and $D$ are conformable for multiplication:

$$
\underset{\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} \times \color{green}{\fbox{3}}}{C} \underset{\color{green}\checkmark}{\cdot} \underset{{\color{green}\fbox{3}} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}}{D} = 
	\underset{\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}}{CD}
$$

Let's compute $CD,$ one element at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}], &  & \,-4=1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 2+0\cdot (-3) \\  & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}], &  & \,1=1\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0+0\cdot 2 \\  & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ -1 & ∗\end{aligned}], &  & \,-1=2\cdot 0+1\cdot 2+1\cdot (-3) \\  & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}], &  & \,4=2\cdot 1+1\cdot 0+1\cdot 2\end{aligned}
$$
